newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong pendulum swings towards China.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong pendulum swings towards China.

text.p: Governor Chris Patten on Tuesday presided over the last cabinet meeting of British rule east of Suez as Hong Kong's pendulum of rule swung ever faster back to China.
In a sign of the new reality, Britain had just bowed to Chinese demands to send more than 500 armed troops into Hong Kong before colonial rule ends.

The troops would drive into Hong Kong at 9 p.m. (1300 GMT) on June 30 -- anticipating the midnight end of Britain's 156 years of rule by three hours -- to ensure security and a smooth handover, officials said.

London had at first stoutly resisted the move, insisting it was the sovereign power until the final retreat was ceremonially beaten by its massed military bands, but yielded to forceful arguments by Beijing that the troops were needed to ensure the safety of Chinese President Jiang Zemin at the handover.

A British government spokesman put a brave face on the climbdown, which pointed up the increasing irrelevance of British views with only a week to go before the sun finally sets on an empire that once spanned the globe.
"This is not a concession. As diplomats we try to come up with solutions," the spokesman said after protracted negotiations with the Chinese.
But one diplomatic analyst close to the talks said: "This shows Britain has no cards left to play against China in Hong Kong. Britain had to face reality."
Hong Kong's elected Legislative Council, which goes out of existence to be replaced by a Beijing-appointed legislature next week, puts its own brave face on the future.
Legislators debated and passed bills that were purely symbolic because on July 1 they will be null and void.
"All this fuss about whether the Chinese can send a few more troops over the border before the handover has nothing to do with military security. There's no threat to Hong Kong," one analyst said.
"It's about the end of British sovereignty and the start of China's. It's all political."
The last meeting of Patten's 10-member Executive Council, or cabinet, was solely a ceremonial affair with farewells, not decisions, the order of the day.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index, barometer of business confidence in this capitalist enclave facing an uncertain future under communist rule, made a shaky start to the day.

The blue-chip index was down 0.79 percent to 14,902 points in morning trade, with sentiment hurt by Beijing's announcement last week of new guidelines on "red chips" -- Hong Kong-based companies with financial backing from China.
Almost 200 unarmed People's Liberation Army (PLA) troops are already in Hong Kong to set up facilities for the main military force.
On June 30, 509 troops in 39 passenger vehicles will enter Hong Kong. Over the next few months the garrison is expected to build up to several thousand.

A senior Chinese representative on the Sino-British Joint Liaison Group, Chen Zuo'er, said the troops on handover night would carry light weapons -- rifles and side arms -- and would not travel in armoured vehicles.
There was no suggestion the Chinese precautions indicated any threat to the handover ceremonies.
Taiwan on Monday had kicked off high-profile war games seen by some as provocative ahead of China's takeover.
Taipei has said the timing of its two-day "Chinese glory" drills, announced a year ago, had nothing to do with Hong Kong's handover.
Commanders made clear, however, that the exercises had everything to do with mainland China and its intensifying drive to isolate the island it regards as a renegade province.
Once Hong Kong is firmly under its control, Beijing is expected to apply even more pressure to bring Taiwan back into the traditional Chinese empire.
